newsitem.title: UK: Slow EMU transtition could cost insurers - report.
newsitem.headline: Slow EMU transtition could cost insurers - report.

text.p: The European insurance industry could find it costly to adopt the Euro over three years rather than directly from its initial introduction, according to an industry report.

A document published by the London International Insurance And Reinsurance Market Association (LIRMA) said a key question was: "whether or not the insurance industry in the EU will try to go for a big bang approach and use the Euro exclusively from day one. A transition period of three years could be very costly for all concerned."
The report was based on talks with banks in the UK, the U.S, and Europe, in response to a request from LIRMA on the implications of monetary union on London-based insurers.
It advised that members assume EMU will come into effect as planned on January 1, 1999, but that sterling will not participate before 2002 at the earliest.
LIRMA believes the retail insurers in particular will face high costs if they have to operate parallel quoting, transaction, and settlement systems in existing currencies as well as the Euro.

LIRMA chief executive Marie-Louse Rossi told Reuters: "Assuming monetary union goes ahead, LIRMA would like the transition period to be as short as possible to keep down costs. We have been working with the Bank of England and have briefed it fully on our views."

The report advised treasurers of insurance companies to be more proactive with their banks in exploring the types of instruments they will need to replace to get maximum benefit from the enhanced environment for investments and hedging instruments expected to follow monetary union.
"These discussions should not wait until a decision is taken on whether the UK is 'in' or 'out', as that will be only one factor in the whole scenario." the report said.
It pointed out that whether the UK adopts the Euro or not, the nature and risk of different types of investments will change dramatically, for example if interest rates drop.

"Careful attention will need paying to how best to anticipate the effects on markets of the different components of the EMU countries in order to match assets to insurance liabilities," the report added.

The report also advised that changes would be need to the system which settle the cost of insurance transactions between banks, and the London Processing Centre, which handles electronic insurance placings for London.
